title: Resources for Contractors | Genstone Construction
metaDescription: Resources for Genstone contractor partners: photo and documentation standards, lien waivers, draw requests, scheduling and state-specific waiver forms.
lede: Built for the pros who build with us. Explore practical resources, standards and support designed to help Genstone contractor partners work smarter and grow their business, from how to document a job and request a draw to how lien waivers and scheduling work on projects for investors, rental owners and institutional clients.

sections.body: Here are resources and information for our current contractor partners. The sections below explain the working standards that apply on Genstone projects. Your project manager is the first stop for questions about a specific job, and the Contractor FAQs cover common questions about the network itself.

Many Genstone clients manage their properties from another city, and institutional clients report on every asset they own. For most of them, your photos are the only way they see the work. Good documentation also supports draw requests and protects you if a question comes up later.

- Before photos. Document every room and area in the scope before work starts, plus the exterior, mechanicals and any existing damage.
- Progress photos. Capture each significant stage, especially work that will be covered: framing, rough plumbing, rough electrical, insulation, waterproofing and subfloor repairs.
- Hidden conditions. If demolition reveals something outside the scope, stop, photograph it before anything is repaired or covered, and notify your project manager.
- Completion photos. Show each finished scope item, taken from the same angles as the before photos where possible.
- Make photos useful. Take them in good light, wide enough to show where in the house you are, with close-ups where detail matters. Label them by room and scope item.

Keep inspection results and permit records with the photos.

A lien waiver is a document in which a contractor, subcontractor or supplier gives up some or all of its right to file a mechanics' lien against a property, usually in exchange for payment. Waivers protect property owners from paying for work twice, and they keep a property's title clear for sale or refinance.

Waivers generally come in two types. A conditional waiver takes effect only once the payment it describes is actually received. An unconditional waiver takes effect when signed, so it should only be signed after payment has cleared. Both types also come in partial versions, covering a progress payment, and final versions, covering the whole job.

Some states require specific statutory waiver forms, and rules differ from state to state. On Genstone projects, you'll provide waivers for work you've been paid for and make sure your own subcontractors and suppliers are paid and provide theirs.

These lien waivers are provided as a courtesy for use by contractors currently working with Genstone Construction. Any other use is prohibited. Use the form for the state where the property is located, not the state where your business is based, and ask your project manager if you aren't sure which form applies.

Genstone manages client billing and contractor payments according to the approved project scope, required documentation and the applicable draw or payment schedule. Draws are tied to completed work. That structure is the same one many investors' lenders use, which is why the documentation behind a draw request matters.

A clean draw request:

- Matches the milestones in the approved scope and draw schedule.
- Covers only work that's actually complete. Partially finished items generally wait for the next draw.
- Includes completion photos for each item in the request.
- Includes any required inspection sign-offs for that stage.
- Includes lien waivers for previously paid work, from you and from your subs and suppliers as required.
- Leaves out unapproved extras. Work outside the scope needs an approved, documented change order before it can be billed.

Missing photos and waivers are the most common reasons a draw is held up.

Every day a project stays open costs an investor money in interest, insurance, taxes and utilities, and an institutional client tracks timelines across many properties. Each project includes a construction schedule with anticipated milestones, reviewed with the client before work begins.

What keeps a schedule on track:

- Start when committed, and keep the job staffed so it doesn't sit idle between trades.
- Order long-lead materials early. Cabinets, windows and special-order items are frequent causes of delay.
- Sequence for inspections, so rough-in inspections happen before insulation and drywall and nothing has to be torn open.
- Plan around weather for exterior work, roofing and concrete.
- Tell your project manager early when something threatens a milestone. A known delay can be managed with the client. A surprise one usually can't.

sections.h2: Working with occupied and vacant properties
sections.body: Genstone projects include occupied rentals, vacant investor properties and bank-owned homes, and each calls for a little different handling. In an occupied unit, confirm access times through your project manager, protect the tenant's belongings and floors, keep the work area secure at the end of each day, and leave water and power on whenever possible. At a vacant or REO property, secure the house every time you leave, report signs of break-in, leaks or pest activity right away, and keep lockbox codes and access details private under your non-disclosure agreement.

If you need a resource that isn't listed here, ask your Genstone project manager. Contractors interested in joining the network can start with the Pre-Application Checklist and the Contractor Application.
